title: Do We Really Get More Set in Our Ways With Age?
metaTitle: Do We Really Get More Set in Our Ways With Age?
metaDescription: Partly true, but overstated. Openness declines modestly and habits deepen, yet the brain stays plastic and rigidity with age is not inevitable.
keyFinding: Openness tends to decline modestly with age and habits deepen, but the stereotype of becoming rigid with age is overstated — adults keep learning and changing throughout life.
honestAnswer: Partly — but considerably less than the stereotype suggests. There is some real basis for it: the personality trait of Openness to experience tends to decline modestly from young adulthood onward, which can mean a bit less novelty-seeking and a bit more preference for the familiar, and habits do tend to deepen the longer we repeat them. Those are genuine, measurable tendencies.

But 'set in your ways' as a fixed law of aging is not what the evidence supports. The adult brain retains meaningful plasticity, older adults clearly can and do learn new things and change their minds, and the belief itself is partly a self-fulfilling stereotype. The honest picture is a gentle drift, not a hardening — and one that is far from inevitable.
whatDataShows: Large studies of personality change across the lifespan, summarised in work by Roberts and by Soto and colleagues, find that Openness to experience tends to rise into young adulthood and then decline gradually across the rest of life on average. Openness is the trait most associated with curiosity, imagination, and appetite for the new, so a modest decline can show up as somewhat less novelty-seeking and a greater comfort with the familiar.

Habit research, including work associated with Wendy Wood, helps explain the rest. Behaviours that are repeated in stable contexts become increasingly automatic over time, running with less conscious deliberation. Decades of repeated routines naturally produce deeply grooved habits — which can look, from the outside, like rigidity but are really the ordinary mechanics of how habits form.

Against this sits a substantial body of work on neuroplasticity in adulthood: the brain continues to form and reshape connections in response to learning and experience well beyond youth. Older adults routinely acquire new skills, languages, and ideas. So while change may come with more friction, the capacity for it persists across the lifespan.
whyItFeelsDifferent: The stereotype feels truer than it is partly because deep habits are highly visible while quiet change is not. Someone's decades-old routines are obvious; the new things they have learned or the views they have revised are far less so. We notice the grooves and miss the growth.

There is also a self-fulfilling element. If people expect to become rigid with age — and expect it of others — they may seek out less novelty and try fewer new things, which then produces exactly the inflexibility the stereotype predicted. The belief can help create the outcome it describes.

And a modest average decline in Openness is easy to over-read. 'Slightly less novelty-seeking, on average, across a population' is a much weaker claim than 'people become closed-minded as they age,' but the stronger version is the one that sticks, because it fits a familiar cultural story about getting older.
whatResearchSaysToDo: The most useful implication is that flexibility appears to be something that can be maintained rather than simply lost. Because the brain stays plastic and learning remains possible throughout adulthood, deliberately continuing to seek out new experiences, skills, and viewpoints works with the evidence rather than against it.

Treating habits as adjustable rather than fixed also helps. Habit research suggests that changing context and surroundings is one of the more effective levers for reshaping automatic behaviour, since stable contexts are what entrench habits in the first place. Deep routines are not permanent; they respond to changed circumstances.

Finally, the research on stereotypes of aging suggests that holding a more accurate, less fatalistic view of your own capacity to change is itself worthwhile, because expectations can shape behaviour. Assuming you can still learn and adapt tends to support actually doing so.
whatDoesNotHelp: Accepting 'I'm just set in my ways now' as a fixed fact tends not to help, and the evidence does not support it as one. Treating a gentle, average decline in Openness as a hard limit can become a self-fulfilling prediction that reduces the very flexibility you assume you have lost.

Relying only on willpower to override a deeply grooved habit is a common but weak strategy. Habit research suggests that established behaviours in stable contexts are run automatically, so trying to out-muscle them through resolve alone, without changing the surrounding context, usually underperforms.

Assuming that the capacity to learn and change simply switches off at some age is also a misreading. Neuroplasticity research indicates the brain keeps adapting throughout adulthood; change may take more effort and repetition, but the door does not close.
realNumbersInContext: The personality side of this is best understood as a trend, not a cliff. Lifespan studies (Roberts, Soto and colleagues) describe Openness peaking around young adulthood and then declining gradually on average across later decades — a real but modest shift, with wide individual variation, rather than a uniform hardening that applies to everyone.

The habit and plasticity findings provide the counterweight. Habit research suggests behaviours become automatic with repeated practice in stable settings, which is why long-standing routines feel so fixed; and neuroplasticity research consistently shows the adult brain continues to rewire with learning. Taken together, the numbers describe gentle drift plus deep habits — not the closed-minded inevitability the stereotype implies.

keyTakeaways: Openness to experience tends to decline modestly from young adulthood on — a gentle drift, not a hardening.
Long-repeated behaviours in stable contexts become automatic, which can look like rigidity but is just how habits form.
The adult brain stays plastic: older adults clearly can and do learn new things and change their minds.
The stereotype is partly self-fulfilling — expecting rigidity can lead people to seek less novelty and become less flexible.
Changing your context works better than willpower for reshaping deeply grooved habits.

examples.label: The mechanism
examples.title: Grooved habits look like rigidity from the outside
examples.body: Someone's decades-old routines — the same breakfast, the same route, the same order of doing things — are highly visible, while the new skills they have picked up or the views they have quietly revised are not. We notice the grooves and miss the growth, so ordinary automaticity gets read as a closed mind.

examples.label: Illustrative
examples.title: 'I'm just set in my ways now'
examples.body: Treating a modest, average decline in Openness as a hard personal limit tends to become a self-fulfilling prediction: expecting rigidity, you try fewer new things, and the flexibility you assumed you'd lost quietly erodes. The more accurate frame — that the brain stays plastic and change is still possible with more repetition — works with the evidence rather than against it.

faqs.question: Do people actually become less open-minded with age?
faqs.answer: On average, Openness to experience tends to decline modestly from young adulthood onward, which can mean slightly less novelty-seeking. But this is a gentle population-level trend with wide individual variation, not a rule that people become closed-minded — and it is far weaker than the stereotype suggests.

faqs.question: Can older adults still learn new things?
faqs.answer: Yes. Research on neuroplasticity shows the adult brain keeps forming and reshaping connections in response to learning throughout life. Acquiring new skills may take more repetition and effort with age, but the capacity to learn and change persists.

faqs.question: Why do my habits feel so hard to break as I get older?
faqs.answer: Habit research suggests behaviours repeated in stable contexts become increasingly automatic over time, so decades of routine produce deeply grooved habits. They can feel fixed, but they are not permanent — changing your surrounding context is one of the more effective ways to reshape them.

faqs.question: Is 'set in your ways' just a stereotype?
faqs.answer: Partly. There is a real basis — a modest decline in Openness and deeper habits — but the strong version of the stereotype is overstated. It also appears to be partly self-fulfilling: expecting rigidity with age can lead people to seek less novelty, producing the very inflexibility they assumed was inevitable.

faqs.question: How can I stay flexible as I age?
faqs.answer: The evidence points to deliberately continuing to seek out new experiences, skills, and viewpoints, since the brain stays plastic throughout adulthood. For entrenched habits specifically, changing your context tends to work better than willpower alone, because stable contexts are what entrench habits in the first place.
